column3: The same speaker cites clear proofs and warns that God does not guide the excessive liar, directly framing 40:34's final description.
Its barrier and destabilizing doubt show the terminal enclosure of the same murib doubt named in the focus.
A people reject their prophet's call while remaining in troubling doubt, closely paralleling the focus's response to Joseph's proofs.
Moses brings clear proofs, yet his people turn to idolatry; this is a close precedent for rejecting proof after its arrival.
The believing man warns his people through the precedent of earlier confederates, introducing the historical warning developed in the focus.
Their repeated cry persists until destruction, illustrating the outcome of entrenched refusal but not the focus's doubt or messenger sequence.
Those demanding a special sign are confronted with earlier messengers who came with clear proofs, directly exposing rejection despite evidence.
Dispute over Moses's book culminates in troubling doubt, a close doubt pattern without the focus's Joseph or succession setting.
It repeats the Moses-book dispute and troubling doubt, clarifying persistent uncertainty after revelation but not prophetic succession.
Successive messengers bring clear proofs, yet some are denied and killed; it strongly contextualizes the claim that no messenger would follow Joseph.
The same-surah warning invokes recurring peoples and outcomes, supplying nearby historical-precedent context.
Earlier peoples receive messengers with clear proofs and answer with rejection and troubling doubt, closely matching the focus's structure.
It recalls a failure concerning Joseph, but the brothers' family predicament does not clarify Joseph's proofs or the people's doubt.
The command to cast a stubborn disbeliever into Hell supplies a consequence backdrop for the focus's excessive doubter.
It makes the sending of a messenger a condition before punishment, directly illuminating the focus's concern over whether another messenger would be sent.
Messengers after earlier ones bring clear proofs, but prior denial blocks faith and marks transgressors' hearts, closely paralleling the focus.
The same surah points to earlier peoples seized for sins, supplying the historical consequence behind the believer's warning.
It simply affirms that Muhammad is among the messengers and adds little to the focus's proof-and-doubt sequence.
Messengers bring clear proofs, but prior denial prevents belief and seals hearts, closely clarifying sustained doubt after evidence.
The verse joins transgression with troubling doubt, directly echoing the focus's description of the excessive doubter.
It directly refutes denial of resurrection, a related form of disbelief though not the focus's rejection of a messenger after Joseph.
Joseph's brothers propose eliminating him, offering narrative background for Joseph but not his later prophetic evidence.
The Quran is affirmed as a detailed revelation without doubt, providing a positive counterpart to doubting what has come from God.
It declares the Hour certain and God as raiser of those in graves, directly countering doubt about God's future sending and action.
The same surah describes idolaters' later admission of loss and divine misguidance, a nearby consequence of disbelief.
It explicitly locates people in doubt about meeting their Lord, a central form of the focus's doubt.
The sending of the she-camel as a test is a sending motif, but it does not clarify prophetic proof or persistent doubt.
It reports the assumption that God would send no one, closely echoing the focus's claim that no messenger would follow Joseph.
Hud's people deny having received clear proof and refuse to leave inherited gods, a direct parallel to resisting prophetic evidence.
It identifies people as doubtful and blind regarding the Hereafter, related to the focus's doubt but in a different setting.
The arrival of truth and the individual consequences of guidance or error give a broad counterpart to the focus's call and misguidance.
People answer the certain promise of the Hour with conjecture and lack of certainty, directly exemplifying the doubt opposed in the focus.
God's power to create and raise all people as one soul supports the possibility of future divine sending, though indirectly.
The brothers' accusation and Joseph's concealed reaction do not clarify his proofs, the people's doubt, or messenger succession.
Those who doubted and were deceived until God's command arrived show doubt as a sustained, fatal inner condition.
The reference to the most wretched one rising up does not clarify the focus's prophetic or doubt themes.
The family continues remembering Joseph, but this emotional recollection is not related to his clear proofs or public rejection.
It links doubt, diseased hearts, and wrongdoing in refusing divine judgment, clarifying the moral condition of the focus's doubter.
Conflicting claims about a messenger are characterized as doubt without knowledge, a related but distinct instance of murib uncertainty.
The verse contrasts believers' certainty with the doubting response to divine signs and states that God guides or leaves astray, closely supporting the focus.
It declares the revealed Book free of doubt, a positive counterpart to remaining doubtful about what has come.
God gives life, causes death, and gathers people on a doubtless Day, directly contradicting doubts about His future action.
It states that a town is not destroyed before a messenger recites God's signs to it, directly clarifying the role of messenger and evidence.
Disbelievers reject God's signs and question renewed resurrection, a direct example of denial after evidence.
The warning that defrauders should expect resurrection supplies an indirect corrective to denial of future accountability.
It explicitly distinguishes belief in the Hereafter from doubt about it, directly clarifying the focus's state of doubt.
The conditional doubt concerns legal testimony during a will and does not illuminate revelation, Joseph, or prophetic succession.
Hearts that doubt God and the Last Day remain wavering in that doubt, closely depicting the sustained uncertainty of the focus.
Attributing a setback to the people's own conduct does not clarify the focus's proof, doubt, or messenger themes.
Creation of the heavens and earth demonstrates power to recreate humanity at a fixed, doubtless term, an indirect counter to denial.
Doubt about the revealed reminder before punishment parallels resistance to what has come, though without the focus's clear-proof setting.
It records the emphatic claim that God will not raise the dead and directly refutes it as a true divine promise.
The etiquette of not advancing before God and His messenger does not clarify doubt after clear proofs.
God sends a messenger to recite signs and teach a formerly astray people, providing a positive model of the mission rejected in the focus.
It identifies signs in the story of Joseph, offering broad Joseph context without addressing his prophetic proofs in Egypt.
A true revelation is sent to warn a people lacking a prior warner, related to the focus's concern about messenger succession.
God's certain gathering on the Day of Resurrection supplies a firm counterpoint to the focus's skeptical future claim.
The demand to see God openly before believing illustrates refusal to accept mediated evidence, though in a different episode.
The Prophet's lack of prior reading or writing blocks a specific ground for doubting revelation, directly clarifying doubt about a delivered message.
It defines the messenger's mission as mercy, a broad positive account of the sending rejected by the focus's people.
The dispute about joining a campaign and altering God's word does not illuminate Joseph's proofs or persistent doubt.
Messengers confront doubt in God while hearers demand clear authority and defend inherited worship, closely paralleling resistance to prophetic proof.
Universal resurrection and full accounting supply an eschatological consequence for doubting God's future action.
A messenger recites signs, purifies, and teaches a people formerly in manifest error, a positive counterpart to resisting a messenger.
Jesus is made an example for Israel, but this does not meaningfully clarify the focus's doubt or claim about a later messenger.
The dispatch of devils to prod disbelievers offers a broad misguidance backdrop, not the focus's evidence-and-doubt relation.
Clear proof is set as the basis on which one perishes or lives, reinforcing the accountability of response to evidence.
The destruction of stronger earlier peoples supplies a historical-warning counterpart to the focus's recurring-precedent language.
The dead person's rejected request to return and act rightly, followed by the barrier until resurrection, clarifies the finality of delayed response.
The command to remember a covenant and obey does not specifically illuminate the focus's doubt after proofs.
The question about Saqar supplies only a general punishment setting for the excessive doubter.
People divide after knowledge arrives, and later inheritors remain in troubling doubt; this closely shows doubt persisting despite received knowledge.
Inheritance provisions and a legal use of death do not clarify the focus's themes.
Shared belief in one God and revelation provides only a broad contrast to the focus's doubtful rejection.
Noah's explicit warning to his people supplies a basic prophetic-mission counterpart, though without the focus's proof and doubt pattern.
The same divine sign leads some to faith and others to question its intent, while God leaves defiantly disobedient people astray.
Recitation and prayer restrain wrongdoing, offering an indirect alternative to the excess named in the focus.
Messengers bring clear proofs to their peoples and criminals are punished, strongly paralleling proof, rejection, and consequence.
Household etiquette and marriage restrictions do not clarify the focus's message, doubt, or succession themes.
The repeated mocking of every arriving prophet illustrates persistent collective rejection of prophetic sending.
It plainly describes people as playing while in doubt, directly reinforcing the focus's characterization of sustained doubt.
Israel's rejection of signs, killing of prophets, and transgression offer a distant precedent but not a focused relation to Joseph's proofs.
It makes the Hour a sign and commands that it not be doubted, directly countering eschatological doubt.
It merely identifies Elijah as a messenger and adds little to the focus's proof-and-doubt sequence.
Birth, death, and resurrection are joined in one person's story, supporting future raising but not the focus's prophetic rejection.
Later people inhabit the dwellings of self-wrongers and are shown how they were treated, reinforcing the focus's historical warning.
Multiple messengers are sent and denied, directly illustrating the recurring pattern of refusing those sent by God.
Noah's limits of knowledge and authority do not clarify the focus's clear proofs or persistent doubt.
The Quran's imagined effect on a mountain is a broad contrast to human failure to respond to revelation.
It simply names Lot as a messenger and adds little to the focus's proof, doubt, or succession themes.
Moses's condemnation of magic does not clarify doubt about prophetic evidence or later messenger sending.
Those raised by God continue to swear falsely, showing that entrenched falsehood can persist into the resurrection setting.
The earth's earthquake signals the final event but does not clarify the focus's specific doubt or messenger claim.
Moses and Aaron are sent with signs and clear authority, a close positive example of prophetic evidence.
The general statement that criminals are treated thus offers only a remote consequence context.
True believers do not fall into doubt after believing in God and His messenger, directly contrasting the focus's excessive doubter.
The Quran is sent as guidance with clear proofs, a positive counterpart to failing to receive clear proofs rightly.
The denial of having been sent as watchers is a different use of sending and does not clarify prophetic mission.
The contrast between two ways of walking does not specifically illuminate the focus's doubt or messenger sequence.
A constructed institution remains troubling doubt in hearts until death, directly portraying self-sustaining, entrenched doubt.
Earlier peoples' messengers came with clear proofs, yet they disbelieved and were seized; this is an immediate same-surah parallel to 40:34.
Moses is sent to Pharaoh with God's signs and clear authority, supplying the surrounding Egyptian-prophetic pattern in which 40:34 is spoken.
The direct continuation identifies those who dispute God's signs without authority and says God seals every arrogant tyrant's heart, explaining the focus's misguidance of the excessive doubter.
Those disputing God's signs without authority are driven by inaccessible pride; this develops the same-surah motive behind refusing proof.
The question about those disputing God's signs returns to the same resistance-to-revelation theme, though it adds less than 40:35.
Denying the Book and what God sent His messengers with directly describes rejection of the evidence recalled in the focus.
Moses and Aaron come to Pharaoh and his chiefs with signs, giving a close Egyptian precedent for proof delivered to a resistant people.
Pharaoh is described as exalted and excessive, directly echoing the focus's designation of the misled person as excessive.
Pharaoh is shown all the signs but denies and refuses them, a compact and direct pattern of rejecting clear evidence.
When Moses comes with manifest signs, they call them fabricated magic and deny them, closely clarifying response to clear proofs.
Joseph rejects the religion of people who disbelieve in God and the Hereafter, supplying his own stated prophetic stance behind the focus's reference to him.
Joseph calls to worship God alone and identifies this as the established religion, but notes that most people do not know; it gives the content of his call.
The Prophet's call upon clear insight provides a positive counterpart to the clear proofs that Joseph's people failed to receive rightly.
The sequence of death, life, death, renewed life, and return to God directly grounds divine power over the future action doubted in the focus.
Those struck dead are revived so that they may give thanks, making resurrection a demonstrated sign rather than an unsupported claim.
God brings the dead to life and shows His signs, directly connecting revivification with evidentiary disclosure.
The revival of the dead man and his provision is made a sign for people, a concrete counterexample to doubt about resurrection.
Jesus brings a sign by giving life to the dead by God's permission, linking prophetic evidence with God's power over death.
The objection that bones and fragments could become a new creation is a direct form of the future-denial represented in the focus.
The question of who can restore even the most resistant imagined form receives the answer that the original Creator can, directly rebutting resurrection doubt.
Human creation, death, and revival of dead earth are presented as visible grounds for certainty in resurrection.
God is declared the truth and the One who gives life to the dead, explicitly establishing the reality that doubt contests.
Human death is followed by resurrection on the Day of Rising, directly supplying the future sequence denied by skeptical hearers.
It explicitly states that people will be raised on the Day of Resurrection, a concise answer to denial of God's future sending.
The claim that a person who dies and becomes dust and bones cannot be brought forth closely parallels the focus's rejection of future divine action.
The assertion that there is only worldly life and no resurrection presents the same denial in a broader materialist form.
People deny resurrection after themselves and their forefathers have become dust and bones, closely matching persistent rejection of the promise.
The resurrection promise is dismissed as an old tale, showing how inherited refusal can persist despite repeated warning.
The trumpet summons people from graves to their Lord, directly depicting the raising that doubters deny.
The objector asks who can revive decayed bones while forgetting his own creation, a classic direct formulation of resurrection doubt.
The answer that the first Creator will revive decayed bones directly resolves the objection raised in 36:78 and the focus's skeptical claim.
Reviving the dead earth is offered as a sign that God will give life to the dead, an explicit evidentiary analogy for resurrection.
God revives dead land with measured water and says people will likewise be brought forth, directly connecting a sign to future raising.
The deniers reduce life and death to time and deny knowledge beyond conjecture, closely matching the focus's settled doubt masquerading as certainty.
When clear signs are recited, the deniers answer by demanding the return of their forefathers, directly displaying refusal after evidence.
The claim that return after becoming dust is too remote is a direct resurrection objection of the same kind as the focus's denial of future sending.
Those who doubt a new creation after the first creation embody the recurring uncertainty that the focus attributes to its hearers.
The question whether God will not gather bones articulates a concise form of resurrection doubt.
The Creator who formed human beings from a drop is explicitly declared able to give life to the dead, directly refuting denial of resurrection.
Those who ask whether they will really be returned to a former state give another direct voice to the resurrection skepticism at issue.
The doubted return is described as occurring through a single cry, contrasting divine ease with human disbelief.
